name: Nora Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no employer or AI-company ties. Your answers are confidential. How does a normal workday go?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Nora Weber, fifty-eight, and I'm a junior accountant at Mill Yard Ledger, checking builders' invoices and tax returns. I like finding the one invoice that makes an account balance; retyping a supplier name after a poor scan tests my patience. My partner Eli works in a warehouse, and our grown children call on Sundays rather than pay our bills.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to the accounts desk?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I earned a bachelor's degree in accounting after other office jobs, and I am still learning the trickier tax cases. I use AI now and then only after colleagues test it, mainly for draft reminder notes, and I check every amount myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau — Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team at Mill Yard Ledger that a small tool saving on sorting is fine if the invoice still matches the supplier statement. The customer shouldn't have to find our error first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am a junior on the contractors' tax desk, and I am still learning the odd tax cases, but I get a normal wage for the work. My partner and I have about five months of expenses saved, so I don't expect a small sorter to take the job; we still need the wage as retirement comes closer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reconciling builders' invoices against supplier statements and use our tested AI note tool only for first drafts of reminder emails. I'd take the next tricky tax adjustment to my supervisor before we submit it, just as I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the present wage, though I keep an eye on the savings account. Five months is a helpful cushion, not an income for the years ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you enjoy at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like finding the one invoice that explains why a small builder's total is out. I don't enjoy copying the same supplier name three times after a poor scan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you learn the work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I earned a bachelor's degree in accounting later and came in as a junior, so I'm still building speed. I use AI now and then after a colleague tests it, but I check every amount against the statement myself.

say: I'd keep **invoice checks** against original supplier statements before each return is signed.
I'd use the **tested note tool** only for draft reminders to contractors.
think: My **junior wage** seems steady in this mild picture of small tool changes.
Five months saved cannot replace **future income** as retirement comes closer.
do: Keep **contractor invoices** matched to original supplier statements before filing returns.
Ask my **supervisor** to review unusual tax adjustments before the next filing deadline.
S0.quote: The customer shouldn't have to find our error first.
fieldNote: Her **occasional tested AI notes** and supervisor checks are existing routines, not a new training plan.
Typical junior pay and **five months saved** cover today, but the reserve cannot fund retirement by itself.

steps.text: Keep reconciling contractor invoices against supplier statements
Seek supervisor review before filing unusual contractor tax adjustments

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption — Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mill Yard to show the team which contractor errors the new system makes and which paid hours remain for juniors. I don't mind a tool that has been tested, but I want the mistake count on the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A program can read invoices and draft returns, which is a lot of my junior day. I could lose pay before I have learned the harder cases, and five months saved would not cover a long search at fifty-eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a paid supervised demonstration on closed supplier statements if the partners approve it, then use the new matching screen only if its missed-error and repair-time figures hold up. In the first year of steady change, if Mill Yard cuts my paid week below four days, I'd apply for posted junior billing jobs at the nearby transport firms while keeping paid Mill Yard work until a written bill-covering wage and start date are confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing part of my own wage. Being willing to learn does not guarantee the firm keeps a junior place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the demonstration is unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay with the approved note tool and ask the supervisor for a written paid-hours plan. I wouldn't put a contractor's live statements into a new system at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you test on the closed statements?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd count missed invoices, duplicate payments and the minutes it takes to fix them. If those figures are worse than our checks now, I'd say so to the partners before live use.

say: I'd ask for **missed-error figures** from the new system and paid junior hours.
I'd accept **supervised learning** only on paid time using closed client files.
think: My **invoice work** could shrink before I master harder cases.
A five-month buffer won't fund a **long wage gap**.
do: Learn the **matching screen** on approved paid supervised time, conditional on error checks.
Apply for **posted transport billing** below four paid days.
Keep **paid Mill Yard work** until written bill-covering outside terms begin.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a shorter paid week.
S1.quote: I wouldn't put a contractor's live statements into a new system at home.
fieldNote: Her **new AI learning** concerns invoice matching and is gated by paid supervision and measured errors, unlike routine draft notes.
A **below-four-day cut** starts search; actual transport postings and written bill-covering wage and start govern a move.

steps.text: Learn matching screen in approved paid supervised closed-file demonstration; use only after error/time checks pass
Keep approved note tool and request written hours plan if demonstration unpaid
Apply to posted transport billing after paid week falls below four days
Keep paid Mill Yard work until written bill-covering outside wage/start

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 — Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell contractors full AGI in 2028 reaches our invoice and tax thinking before robots reach their hands-on sites around 2031. Calling a site visit a safe job would be dishonest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect Mill Yard to cut junior tax posts sharply, perhaps mine. My partner's warehouse wage and five months saved would help with rent and food, but losing my own wage would still hurt before we know what retirement will pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cancel the current sixty-a-month television package and add that money from wages to emergency savings now. In the first year after 2028, if Mill Yard ends my post, I'd apply for advertised paid billing work at the local bus depot, keeping any paid Mill Yard closing entries while offered until a written wage covering our bills and a start date are confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because I expect a large part of our household pay could vanish. Five months of savings gives me a search window, not a new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the bus depot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It has payroll and supplier bills, and I have checked transport invoices before. AGI reaches that desk too, so I would ask for an actual posted role rather than assume public transport protects an office worker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our grown children what happened, but I would not plan on their wages. My partner Eli and I would cut the television bill now, while both wages still arrive. We'd use our own savings for essentials.

say: I'd say **2028 AGI** reaches our desk before 2031 site robots.
I'd ask for **actual paid openings** rather than reassuring labels.
think: I expect my **junior post** may disappear quickly when AGI reaches our invoice desk.
Eli's **warehouse wage** cannot replace mine entirely while we still pay regular bills.
do: Cancel the **television package** and save sixty monthly.
Apply for **posted depot billing** after Mill Yard ends my post.
Keep **paid closing entries** only while offered until written bill-covering terms start.
S2.quote: My partner Eli and I would cut the television bill now, while both wages still arrive.
fieldNote: Nora expects her **own junior role** to face AGI in 2028; physical site robots follow later.
The cancelled package adds **new monthly cash**; depot billing needs an advertised paid vacancy and written bill-covering wage and start.

steps.text: Cancel television package and save sixty monthly from wages
Apply for posted paid bus-depot billing after job loss; require written bill-covering wage/start
Keep paid Mill Yard closing entries only while offered until outside start

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031 — Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the partners five years is long enough to show what the new tools actually miss and to give juniors a paid path into other work. Full AGI reaches the accounts desk in 2031, while robots reach physical site tasks around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can try a new system when someone shows me the errors, but I still need paid work at sixty-three. The bus depot's office is no shelter from AGI; a vacancy there would simply be a chance to keep earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mill Yard next spring for one paid afternoon a month shadowing its supplier-billing team, with their supervisor checking my entries. In the first year after 2031, if my tax post ends, I'd apply for a posted paid billing role at the depot only with a written bill-covering wage and start date, and keep any paid Mill Yard work while offered until that outside job begins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about changing the kind of desk work I do. Five years gives me a chance to practise, but only if the firm pays for the hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Mill Yard refuses the shadowing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the paid tax desk while it lasts and read the depot's posted vacancies. I would not do unpaid billing practice at home or use our five-month buffer for a course nobody requires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a formal course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a posted paid depot job requires a billing module and the employer pays the fee and study hours. I have a bachelor's degree already. I won't sit at a depot desk learning the billing screen for free while our rent waits at home.

say: I'd ask for **paid monthly shadowing** of supplier billing.
I'd distinguish **2031 desk risk** from 2034 site robots.
think: I still need **paid work at sixty-three**.
A depot desk is a **possible vacancy**, not safety from AGI.
do: Shadow **supplier billing** one paid afternoon monthly if approved.
Take a **required billing module** only for a posted paid depot job with funded fees and paid study time.
Apply for **posted depot billing** after tax loss; keep offered Mill Yard pay until written bill-covering wage/start.
feel: I feel **anxious** about needing another desk role.
S3.quote: I won't sit at a depot desk learning the billing screen for free while our rent waits at home.
fieldNote: Her **paid monthly shadowing** is real on-the-job learning only with firm approval and supervisor checks; refusal means keeping paid tax work.
The separate module needs a **posted paid vacancy** and funded fee and paid time; any move needs written bill-covering terms.

steps.text: Shadow supplier billing one paid supervised afternoon monthly only if firm approves
Take required module for posted paid depot job only with funded fees and paid study hours
Apply for posted depot billing after tax post ends; require written bill-covering wage/start
Keep paid Mill Yard work while offered; decline unpaid shadowing if refused

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036 — Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to check what retirement really pays and to keep learning while the firm still has paid work. Full AGI reaches our accounts desk in 2036; robots for hands-on construction follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-eight I may already have stopped work, but that depends on our actual retirement figures, not a story about what people our age receive. If we still need my wage, a junior tax job would face AGI even after a decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request a written retirement-income estimate and compare it with our bills each year, keeping paid Mill Yard accounts work while it is offered. In the first year after 2036, if verified income covers essentials, I'd stay within that budget; if I still need paid work and my tax post ends, I'd apply for posted depot billing only with written bill-covering wage and start, keeping any paid Mill Yard closing work only while offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy because the ten years give us time to get actual figures. I cannot promise that retirement income will be enough, and I would need a paid alternative if it isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire sooner to avoid AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I won't leave the contractor returns until written retirement figures cover our rent and food. I would not stop earning on a guess about pension money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the depot has no vacancy in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take only paid Mill Yard closing work still offered and check other posted billing jobs nearby. We would use savings for essentials while I search; I would not call an interview an income.

say: I'd ask for **verified retirement figures** before promising a date.
I'd name **2036 desk exposure** before 2039 site robots.
think: I may still need a **wage at sixty-eight** if our actual retirement income falls short.
Our **five-month reserve** today cannot prove retirement is affordable for us.
do: Request a **written retirement estimate** and compare it with annual bills.
Keep **paid Mill Yard accounts** while work is offered.
Seek posted depot or **local billing** if wages remain needed after 2036 loss; require written bill-covering pay and start.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about unverified retirement income.
S4.quote: I won't leave the contractor returns until written retirement figures cover our rent and food.
fieldNote: She treats retirement as **conditional on actual figures**, with no assumed pension or grown-child support.
The **2036 paid-work branch** needs a posted depot vacancy and written bill-covering wage and start; Mill Yard pay continues only while offered.

steps.text: Request written retirement estimate and compare with actual household bills yearly
Keep paid Mill Yard accounts while offered; use savings for essentials if work ends
Seek posted depot/local billing if wages needed after 2036 loss; require written bill-covering wage/start

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the junior invoice desk could shrink before I know our retirement income. Paid supervised billing practice and a real posted vacancy with written wages would help, and I'd need notice before my wage stopped.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays for the afternoon spent finding a bad invoice after a system says the return is ready. If the firm wants that check, it has to put paid time on the rota.

headlineQuote: If the firm wants that check, it has to put paid time on the rota.
portrait: Nora, **fifty-eight**, is a junior contractor accountant who likes finding errors and dislikes repeated entry.
She has a **bachelor's degree**, is still learning tax cases and uses tested AI notes occasionally.
Typical pay, **five months saved** and some nearby firms give a finite cushion.
She learns **billing work** only through paid supervision and treats a depot vacancy as conditional.
AGI could end her **junior tax post** before actual retirement income is known.
biggestWorry: She worries most about **AGI by 2028** shrinking her junior wage before retirement figures are clear.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **paid supervised practice**, notice and a posted paid billing vacancy with written terms.
